content: Bloody or tarry stools are often indicative of an injury or disorder within the digestive tract. Physicians may use the term melena to describe black, tarry, and foul-smelling stools, or hematochezia to refer to red or maroon-colored stools. Blood in the stool can originate from any part of the digestive tract, ranging from the mouth to the anus. In some cases, the blood may be present in such small quantities that it is not visible to the naked eye and can only be detected through a fecal occult blood test. When stool appears black, it typically suggests that the bleeding is occurring in the upper gastrointestinal (GI) tract, which includes the esophagus, stomach, and the first portion of the small intestine. Blood exposed to digestive enzymes and acids as it moves through the intestines often takes on a tar-like appearance. Conversely, maroon-colored stools or bright red blood usually indicate bleeding from the lower GI tract, such as the large intestine, rectum, or anus. However, in cases of massive or rapid bleeding in the stomach, bright red stools may also occur. Causes of Bloody or Tarry Stools Upper GI Tract Causes (Black Stools): 1. Abnormal blood vessels (vascular malformations). 2. A tear in the esophagus caused by severe vomiting (Mallory-Weiss tear). 3. Bleeding from stomach or duodenal ulcers. 4. Inflammation of the stomach lining (gastritis). 5. Reduced blood flow to the intestines (bowel ischemia). 6. Trauma or ingestion of a foreign object. 7. Enlarged and dilated veins in the esophagus or stomach (esophageal or gastric varices). Lower GI Tract Causes (Maroon or Bright Red Stools): Bowel ischemia (restricted blood supply to the intestines). 3. Colon polyps or colorectal cancer. 4. Diverticulosis (pouches in the colon wall). 5. Hemorrhoids (a common cause). 6. Inflammatory bowel diseases, such as Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis. 7. Intestinal infections, such as bacterial enterocolitis. 8. Tumors in the small intestine. 9. Trauma or ingestion of a foreign object. 10. Abnormal blood vessel formations (arteriovenous malformations or AVMs). Certain foods and substances can also mimic the appearance of bloody stools. For example, consuming black licorice, lead, iron supplements, bismuth-containing medications (e.g., Pepto-Bismol), or blueberries can cause stools to appear black. Similarly, beets and tomatoes may give stools a reddish hue. In such cases, a chemical test of the stool can confirm whether blood is present. Vomiting blood may also occur in cases of bleeding in the esophagus or stomach, such as with peptic ulcer disease. When to Seek Urgent Medical Care You should contact your doctor immediately if you notice blood in your stool or any changes in stool color. Even if you suspect that hemorrhoids are the cause, a medical evaluation is necessary to rule out more serious conditions. In children, small amounts of blood in the stool are often not serious and are commonly caused by constipation or milk allergies. However, it is still important to inform your doctor, even if further evaluation is not required. Treatment Options If significant blood loss has occurred, emergency treatment may be necessary. This can include: 1. Blood transfusions to replace lost blood. 2. Administration of intravenous fluids. 3. Interventional radiography embolization, a procedure to block bleeding blood vessels. 4. Medications to reduce stomach acid production. 5. Surgery, if bleeding cannot be controlled through other means. Diagnostic Process Your doctor will begin by taking a detailed medical history and performing a physical examination, with a focus on the abdomen and rectum. To better understand the potential causes of bloody or dark stools, your doctor may ask the following questions: Are you taking blood-thinning medications (e.g., aspirin, warfarin, clopidogrel) or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) like ibuprofen or naproxen? Have you experienced any trauma to the abdomen or rectum, or have you accidentally swallowed a foreign object? Have you consumed black licorice, lead, Pepto-Bismol, or blueberries? Have you had more than one episode of blood in your stool? Is every stool affected? Have you experienced recent weight loss? Is the blood only visible on toilet paper? What is the color of the stool? When did the symptoms first appear? Are there any accompanying symptoms, such as abdominal pain, vomiting blood, bloating, excessive gas, diarrhea, or fever? If there is enough blood to visibly alter the appearance of the stool, the color can help pinpoint the source of the bleeding. To confirm a diagnosis, your doctor may use diagnostic tools such as endoscopy or specialized imaging studies. Diagnostic Tests The following tests may be performed to identify the cause and severity of the bleeding: 1. Angiography. 2. Barium studies. 3. Bleeding scans (nuclear medicine imaging). 4. Blood tests, including a complete blood count (CBC), serum chemistries, and clotting studies. 5. Colonoscopy. 6. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD). 7. Stool culture. 8. Tests for Helicobacter pylori infection. 9. Abdominal X-rays. In cases of severe bleeding, hospitalization may be required for close monitoring and evaluation. If the bleeding is massive, intensive care unit (ICU) admission may be necessary. Emergency treatments, such as blood transfusions, may also be administered. Additional Information For further medical care, consult a healthcare provider or visit a hospital equipped to treat conditions involving bloody or tarry stools.
